title: ‘Not anymore’: N.L. judge denies bail to man who bragged about Canada's easy release
summary: Justice Vikas Khaladkar roundly rejected a bail proposal from a man who texted the sister of his former intimate partner, saying: "I’ll get bail. This is Canada. She’ll be with me by the end of the…

image.caption: Justice Vikas Khaladkar said Canada is no longer the same country that gave 'recidivist offenders the benefit of the doubt because of the presumption of innocence' under previous rules on bail. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Justice Vikas Khaladkar roundly rejected a bail proposal from a man who texted the sister of his former intimate partner, saying: "I’ll get bail. This is Canada. She’ll be with me by the end of the day.”
Justice Vikas Khaladkar cites new law in denying bail for repeat offender
A Newfoundland judge has denied bail for a man accused of intimate partner violence who allegedly boasted about how easy it is to get bail in Canada.
Zachary Dunphy is accused of following his former girlfriend into a restaurant washroom, dragging her out by her hair and holding her at knifepoint before fleeing the scene at speeds up to 150 km/h.
It’s alleged he texted the complainant’s sister in the aftermath, saying: “I’ll get bail. This is Canada. She’ll be with me by the end of the day.”
Justice Vikas Khaladkar used Dunphy’s own words against him in a decision rendered on Nov. 4, as he invoked the federal government’s new rules under the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act.
“Not anymore,” Khaladkar wrote of Dunphy's views on Canadian law.

“This is no longer the Canada that gave recidivist offenders the benefit of the doubt because of the presumption of innocence. There are too many instances of persons being released on bail who inflict grievous bodily harm and death on their intimate partners. That is precisely the danger that the Act was intended to stop.”
New legislation puts onus on offenders
The federal Bail and Sentencing Reform Act came into effect in July, and makes release harder to obtain for offenders charged with a broad range of offences, including repeat violent offenders.
Instead of the Crown having to show why an accused person should remain in custody in those cases, the onus is on the offender to prove why they should be released.
In Dunphy's case, the violent nature of the alleged offences and his criminal history put the burden on him to establish why he should be released.
Dunphy was initially denied bail at the provincial court level in May, but applied to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador in October, only to be denied again. (CBC)

Dunphy is scheduled for trial in March on a dozen charges, including forcible confinement, assault with a weapon, choking, dangerous operation of a motor vehicle and failure to comply with a probation order. He has pleaded not guilty.
He was initially denied bail at the provincial court level in May, but applied to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador in October, only to be denied again.
While in custody following the first rejection, Dunphy is alleged to have contacted the complainant and urged her to recant her statements to police, which she later did.
During his time on remand, Dunphy was also charged with attempting to beat a fellow inmate with a broomstick.
The best indication of future performance is past performance.Justice Vikas Khaladkar

Dunphy put forward a bail plan earlier this fall that would see him reside with his parents under the watch of security cameras on the perimeter of their property. His parents pledged to put up $1,000 each, and Dunphy promised to take medication to treat his opioid addiction.
Khaladkar dismissed the plan, noting Dunphy’s brazen remarks about the Canadian justice system and his demonstrated disregard for court conditions.
“In the last eight years there have been 11 occasions upon which the applicant has breached an undertaking or a probation order,” Khaladkar wrote.

“It is clear to me that the best indication of future performance is past performance. Mr. Dunphy has only himself to blame for the fact that he has proven to this court, and other courts, that he does not respect the orders that are imposed upon him.”
Khaladkar said it was clear that Dunphy would reoffend if released from jail.

Dunphy is slated for trial on March 16-17 at the provincial court in St. John’s. He is to remain in custody and abide by a no-contact order prohibiting him from speaking to the complainant and members of her family.
